about: Ohm Toss: four answer rings are painted on the court; toss the beanbag onto the right value. `calc` is the true value in the item's unit; tests/test_gym_games.py checks it matches the answer and no other ring.

items.ask: A 9 V battery drives a 450 Ω resistor. How much current flows?
items.why: I = V / R = 9 / 450 = 0.02 A, which is 20 mA.

items.ask: 15 mA flows through a 200 Ω resistor. What voltage is across it?
items.why: 15 mA is 0.015 A, so V = I × R = 0.015 × 200 = 3 V. Forgetting to convert gives 3000.

items.ask: A resistor has 5 V across it and 2 mA through it. What is its resistance?
1 kΩ, 2 kΩ and 3 kΩ in series on 12 V. What current flows?
items.why: Series resistances add to 6 kΩ. I = 12 / 6000 = 2 mA, the same through every part.

items.ask: 9 V across 2 kΩ and 1 kΩ in series. What is the voltage across the 2 kΩ?
items.why: I = 9 / 3000 = 3 mA, so V = 3 mA × 2 kΩ = 6 V. The bigger resistor takes the bigger share.

items.ask: Two resistors in series on 12 V. One drops 5 V. What does the other drop?
items.why: Around a series loop the drops add up to the supply: 12 − 5 = 7 V.

items.ask: 12 V across 3 kΩ and 6 kΩ in parallel. What is the total current?
items.why: Each branch has the full 12 V: 4 mA through 3 kΩ and 2 mA through 6 kΩ. Branch currents add to 6 mA.

items.ask: Two 4 kΩ resistors in parallel. What is their combined resistance?
items.why: Two equal branches halve the resistance: 4 kΩ / 2 = 2 kΩ. Adding them is the series rule.

items.ask: 9 V across three parallel branches. What is the voltage across the middle branch?
items.why: Every parallel branch sits straight across the supply, so each one sees the full 9 V.

items.ask: A 9 V series loop of R1 and R2, and R2 has a broken lead. How much current flows?
items.why: An open leaves no complete path, so the current is 0 everywhere in the loop.

items.ask: A 9 V series loop of R1 and R2, and R2 is open. What does a meter across R2 read?
items.why: No current means no drop across R1, so all 9 V appears across the gap at R2.

items.ask: A 6 V series loop of three resistors, and one is open. What does a meter across a good resistor read?
items.why: With no current, V = I × R = 0 across every good part. Only the open one reads 6 V.

items.ask: Three 2 kΩ resistors in series on 12 V, and one is shorted. What current flows?
items.why: The short takes one resistor out: 12 / 4 kΩ = 3 mA, up from 2 mA.

items.ask: Three 2 kΩ resistors in series on 12 V, and the middle one is shorted. What does a meter across it read?
items.why: A short is a wire across the part, so it drops 0 V.

items.ask: Three 2 kΩ resistors in series on 12 V, and one is shorted. What does each good resistor read?
items.why: 12 V now splits over two equal resistors: 6 V each, up from 4 V.

items.ask: Labelled 1 kΩ, it has 6 V across it with 3 mA through it. What is its real value?
items.why: R = V / I = 6 / 0.003 = 2000 Ω = 2 kΩ, double the label.

items.ask: Labelled 330 Ω, it reads 3.3 V with 1 mA through it. What is its real value?
items.why: 3.3 / 0.001 = 3300 Ω, ten times the label: a 3.3 kΩ part fitted by mistake.

items.ask: 5 V should push 10 mA through a 500 Ω resistor, but you measure only 5 mA. What is its real value?
items.why: R = 5 / 0.005 = 1000 Ω = 1 kΩ, twice what was planned, so only half the current flows.
